job.style: a step-by-step explanation of a process

passage: When you send a photo to a friend, it does not travel as one single block. Instead, the data is broken into small pieces called packets that take different paths across a global network of interconnected cables and servers. These packets travel through physical infrastructure, including massive undersea fiber-optic cables that use pulses of light to transmit information across oceans, not electricity. Once the data reaches a destination, it is reassembled. Many people mistakenly think the internet is a single central computer, but it is actually a decentralized network of networks owned by many different organizations. When you store files in the cloud, you are simply saving them on physical servers located in large, secure data centers owned by companies, rather than in a magical space. Similarly, your home Wi-Fi is just a local wireless connection to your router, which then connects to your Internet Service Provider. Even if your Wi-Fi is working, the internet connection itself might be down if the provider's network has an issue. Finally, every device connected to the network, including your smart TV or CCTV, is assigned a unique IP address to ensure data reaches the correct destination, though this address identifies the network connection point, not your exact home address.

items.evidence: Instead, the data is broken into small pieces called packets that take different paths across a global network of interconnected cables and servers.
items.q: Meera sends a holiday photo to her friend in Chennai. How does the photo travel?
options: As small pieces that may take different paths
As one whole block along a single path
As pieces that all follow one fixed path
Through the air only, with no cables used
items.explain: The photo is broken into small packets that travel by different paths across cables and servers, then are joined again.

wrong.why: thinks a photo travels as one single block
thinks all packets follow the same path in order
thinks the internet needs no wires anywhere

items.evidence: These packets travel through physical infrastructure, including massive undersea fiber-optic cables that use pulses of light to transmit information across oceans, not electricity.
items.q: How does an email from India usually cross the ocean to reach America?
options: As light pulses in cables under the sea
As electric current in copper wires under the sea
As radio waves through the air, with no wires
Straight to phones by satellite, with no cables
items.explain: Undersea fiber-optic cables carry information across oceans as pulses of light, not electricity.

wrong.why: thinks undersea cables carry electricity in copper
thinks the whole path is through the air
thinks devices connect directly through satellites

items.evidence: Many people mistakenly think the internet is a single central computer, but it is actually a decentralized network of networks owned by many different organizations.
items.q: Riya says one company can switch the whole internet on and off. Which fact shows she is wrong?
options: It is many networks owned by many groups
The government owns it, not any company
Only home routers can switch it off
It is one central computer that never stops
items.explain: The internet is a network of networks owned by many different organizations, so no single owner controls it.

wrong.why: thinks one government owns and controls it
thinks the router makes the internet
thinks the internet is one giant computer

items.evidence: Even if your Wi-Fi is working, the internet connection itself might be down if the provider's network has an issue.
items.q: Aman's phone shows full Wi-Fi bars, but no website opens. What is the most likely reason?
options: His provider's network is having a problem
His phone is broken, because Wi-Fi means internet
His phone needs a satellite signal instead
The one central internet computer is full
items.explain: Wi-Fi only links the phone to the router; if the provider's network has an issue, the internet can be down.

wrong.why: thinks Wi-Fi and the internet are the same
thinks the internet is one central computer

items.evidence: Finally, every device connected to the network, including your smart TV or CCTV, is assigned a unique IP address to ensure data reaches the correct destination, though this address identifies the network connection point, not your exact home address.
items.q: Police find the IP address of a CCTV camera. What can this address tell them?
options: Which network connection point the camera uses
The exact house where the camera's owner lives
Nothing, because cameras do not get IP addresses
The full name of the person who owns it
items.explain: Every connected device, even a CCTV, gets an IP address that shows its network connection point, not an exact home.

wrong.why: thinks an IP address gives an exact home address
thinks only computers and phones have IP addresses
over-generalises that the address identifies a person
